ak_twin_towers.blurb: Twin Towers is a small pair of limestone buttresses on the upper dome of East Grapefruit Rocks, a short drive north of Fairbanks in the interior. Twelve lines are spread across the two towers, a mix of bolted sport climbs, top-rope setups and a few trad routes. The grades run from easy fifth-class climbing in the 5.4 range up to a handful of 5.11 problems, with a good cluster of 5.9 and 5.10 in the middle, so beginners and intermediate leaders both have something to do. The cliff is short, anchors are in place, and the hike up the hillside can be hot and dry on a summer afternoon.

ak_the_left_mandible.blurb: The Left Mandible is a group of cliffs lining the left side of the North Gully at Jaw Point, a coastal tonalite area near Juneau reached by boat. Eleven routes are recorded, mostly traditional lines with two bolted sport climbs. Difficulty starts around 5.9 and climbs through the 5.10s and 5.11s into the 5.12 range, so this is a place for confident leaders rather than beginners. The walls stay shaded early and pick up sun later in the day, and seeps are minor. The terrain is steep and broken into several smaller buttresses reached by a cut trail through alder brush, with a short easy pitch leading to the harder climbing higher up.

ak_service_boulder_anchorage_ak.blurb: Service Boulder is a single granite boulder inside Anchorage, a quick bouldering stop when you do not want to leave town. About eleven problems are logged, and the range is wide: a few easy lines from the lowest grades up to V4 make up most of the traffic, with a pair of far harder projects at the top end. The stone is solid, and the faces are mostly vertical or a bit less, finishing in mantles over small crystals. The short walk in can be confusing because of the web of paths, and summer brings thick mosquitoes, so bug repellent matters.

ak_upper_center_wall.blurb: Upper Center Wall is the higher middle section of the Purinton Creek cliffs, beside the Glenn Highway in the Mat-Su Valley north of Anchorage. Eleven routes, mostly trad with four sport lines, sit on steep and often overhanging ground. Nothing here is easy: grades begin at 5.10, centre on 5.11 and reach into 5.12, so it suits strong leaders. The wall has wide views and is a pleasant spot on a warm afternoon. Getting up is part of the adventure: the right side is reached by scrambling a gully and following a ledge along the cliff, while the left side needs a climb to a belay ledge.

ak_left_wall.blurb: Left Wall is the upper left corner of the main Purinton Creek cliffs, along the Glenn Highway in the Mat-Su Valley. It holds eleven routes, most of them trad, plus a few sport and top-rope lines, on short, steep faces and under large roofs. Grades cluster at 5.10 and 5.12, with one 5.11 and a single 5.13, so expect powerful, overhanging climbing and very little for beginners. Reach it either by scrambling ledges from the crag's bottom-left corner or by leading a pitch on the wall below; most belays carry a bolt, which takes the edge off the exposure.
